Please solve this issue: Our test suite grew big and we haven't noticed how the total RSpec run time outgrew 10 minutes (no parallelization) on CI.

We need to profile the test suite and identify the common problems (shared by many specs) and fix them once and for all. Keep refactoring of individual examples minimal: prefer configuration- and setup-level changes — adding tags, restructuring shared setup, wrapping execution. What the examples assert must stay the same. No app code changes affecting runtime behavior.

NOTE: Running the whole test suite is very time-consuming. Don't try to run the whole test suite (it would fail with timeout due to the Bash tool limitations) or even multiple directories. Only `rspec spec/<some-folder>`. Completely ignore system specs and streaming related specs (we do not run them by default anyway).

We will work on specific spec types at each optimization phase: `spec/models` and `spec/requests`. In the end, we want these two groups together to run at least twice as fast as they do today. Store any insights/comments/plans (such as baseline metrics) that could be useful for the future runs in the docs/ folder (so you can use that knowledge during future optimization runs).

We anticipate a similar speed-up of >30% compared to the baseline (captured at the previous step, before any optimization work). Note that optimizations made for models could have already improved requests specs enough. If that's the case, look for request-specific bottlenecks to get the rest of the way there.

messages.content:
{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output": "# Test Suite Optimization Notes & Plan

## Phase 1: `spec/models` + Global Configuration

### Baseline Metrics (`spec/models` — 1,795 examples)
- **Clean runtime**: `2m 25.1s` (145.1s)
- **RSpecDissect**: `141.5s` total, `116.3s` (82.2%) in setup
- **SQL (`sql.active_record`)**: `113,956` queries (`22.43s`, ~63.5 queries/example)
- **Sidekiq inline jobs (`sidekiq.inline`)**: `3,908` inline job executions (`37.70s` / `26.9%` in EventProf; `42.86s` in `TriggerWebhookWorker` alone across `3,829` calls)
- **Fabrication (`FactoryProf`)**: `4,721` total calls (`3,243` top-level), `126.46s` (`89%` of total time)
  - `status`: `1,003` calls (`68.30s`, `68.1ms`/call)
  - `bookmark`: `1,019` calls (`17` top-level, `34.67s`, `34.0ms`/call — triggered by `Fabricate(:status)` `after_create`)
  - `account`: `1,194` calls (`31.51s`, `26.4ms`/call)
  - `media_attachment`: `40` calls (`6.27s`, `156.7ms`/call)
  - `notification`: `76` calls (`6.42s`, `84.5ms`/call)
  - `user`: `93` calls (`3.51s`, `37.7ms`/call)

### Root Causes Identified
1. **`TriggerWebhookWorker` running inline on every model save (`~30%` of runtime)**:
   - `spec/rails_helper.rb` enabled `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` globally.
   - `Account`, `User`, `Status`, and `Report` `after_commit` callbacks enqueue `TriggerWebhookWorker`.
   - Even with 0 `Webhook` rows in the DB, `TriggerWebhookWorker` reloaded the record from Postgres and serialized the full payload via `REST::Admin::WebhookEventSerializer` before discovering `Webhook.enabled...pluck(:id)` was empty.
   - Out of 1,795 model examples, only 3 failed under `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` — all 3 used `ActionMailer::TestHelper#capture_emails`, which relies on `deliver_later` executing immediately.
2. **Verbose Rails debug/SQL logging in test (`~7.6%` of runtime + 123 MB `log/test.log`)**:
   - `config/environments/test.rb` had no `config.log_level`, defaulting to `:debug`.
   - `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql` formatted, colorized, and wrote every SQL query to `log/test.log`.
3. **Stray `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` in a spec file**:
   - `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb:6` left `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` enabled globally, polluting all subsequent examples with stacktrace collection per SQL query.
4. **Per-example `rails_helper.rb` overhead**:
   - `Rails.application.reload_routes_unless_loaded` ran before every single example (~1.88ms/call, ~3.4s in `spec/models`, ~18s+ across the full suite).
   - `allow(Resolv::DNS).to receive(:open)...` ran `rspec-mocks` setup/teardown before every example.
5. **Repeated DB setup in slow model specs**:
   - Suites like `AccountStatusesCleanupPolicy`, `TagFeed`, `PublicFeed`, `Trends::Statuses`, `Status`, `Notification`, `Status::ThreadingConcern`, `Status::FetchRepliesConcern`, `Account::Interactions`, `Form::Import`, etc. recreated large graphs of `Status`/`Account`/`Tag` records per example via `let`/`let!`/`before`.
   - **Important codebase gotcha for `let_it_be` with `Account`**: `Account` caches `account_stat` association state (`Account::Counters#update_count!` checks `association(:account_stat).loaded?`) AND memoizes relationship ivars (`@following`, `@blocking`, `@muting`, `@domain_blocking`). Use `refind: true` (not `reload: true`) for `let_it_be(:account, ...)` whenever the account may be mutated or queried for relationships.

### Changes Applied in Phase 1
1. **`config/environments/test.rb`**:
   - Set `config.log_level = ENV.fetch('RAILS_LOG_LEVEL', :warn)`.
2. **`spec/rails_helper.rb`**:
   - Required `test_prof/recipes/rspec/let_it_be` (enables `let_it_be` and `before_all`).
   - Moved `Rails.application.reload_routes_unless_loaded` from `config.before` to `config.before :suite`.
   - Replaced per-example `allow(Resolv::DNS).to receive(:open)` mock with a lightweight singleton guard on `Resolv::DNS.open` (respects `type: :system` and `rspec-mocks` stubbing).
   - Added `SidekiqInlineCaptureEmails` wrapping `ActionMailer::TestHelper#capture_emails` in `Sidekiq::Testing.inline!`.
   - Set `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` + `Sidekiq::Worker.clear_all` in `config.before :each, type: :model` (with `:sidekiq_inline` tag opt-in).
3. **`spec/models/**/*_spec.rb` & `spec/support/examples/models/concerns/reviewable.rb`**:
   - Removed stray `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` from `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`.
   - Converted repeated shared setup in the slowest model specs (`account_statuses_cleanup_policy_spec.rb`, `tag_feed_spec.rb`, `public_feed_spec.rb`, `trends/statuses_spec.rb`, `status_spec.rb`, `notification_spec.rb`, `concerns/status/threading_concern_spec.rb`, `concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`, `concerns/account/interactions_spec.rb`, `form/import_spec.rb`, `account_spec.rb`, `account_suggestions/friends_of_friends_source_spec.rb`, `admin/account_action_spec.rb`, `collection_spec.rb`, `concerns/account/mappings_spec.rb`, `form/custom_emoji_batch_spec.rb`, `status/visibility_spec.rb`, `status_pin_spec.rb`, `web/push_subscription_spec.rb`, `account/search_spec.rb`, and `reviewable.rb`) to `let_it_be` / `before_all`.

### Phase 1 Results (`spec/models` — 1,795 examples, 0 failures)
- **Clean runtime**: `145.1s` -> **`40.09s`** (**72.4% faster / 3.62x speedup**)
- **SQL queries**: `113,956` -> `44,916` (**-60.6%**)
- **Factory calls**: `4,721` (`126.46s`) -> `2,809` (`34.66s`) (**-40.5% calls, -72.6% time**)
- **Per-call `status` time**: `68.1ms` -> `27.5ms` (**-60%**)
- **Per-call `account` time**: `26.4ms` -> `13.2ms` (**-50%**)

---

## Plan for Future Phases

### Phase 2: `spec/requests`
1. Profile `spec/requests` baseline (`--profile 25`, `FPROF=1`, `RD_PROF=1`, `EVENT_PROF=sql.active_record`, `EVENT_PROF=sidekiq.inline`).
2. Evaluate extending `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` (or specifically stubbing/faking `TriggerWebhookWorker` unless `:webhooks` / `:sidekiq_inline`) to `type: :request`:
   - In `spec/requests`, many endpoints trigger `Status` / `Account` / `Report` writes, which currently run `TriggerWebhookWorker` inline.
   - Check which request specs rely on inline Sidekiq jobs (e.g., `capture_emails` is already wrapped with `Sidekiq::Testing.inline!`; check `Admin` / `ActivityPub` / `OAuth` request specs).
3. Check `Devise::Test::IntegrationHelpers` / `sign_in` overhead in `type: :request` (see `rails_helper.rb` `SessionActivation` monkey-patch and `let_it_be` for shared users/accounts/tokens/statuses across request examples).

# Test Suite Optimization Notes & Plan

## Phase 1: `spec/models` + Global Configuration

### Baseline Metrics (`spec/models` — 1,795 examples)
- **Clean runtime**: `2m 25.1s` (145.1s)
- **RSpecDissect**: `141.5s` total, `116.3s` (82.2%) in setup
- **SQL (`sql.active_record`)**: `113,956` queries (`22.43s`, ~63.5 queries/example)
- **Sidekiq inline jobs (`sidekiq.inline`)**: `3,908` inline job executions (`37.70s` / `26.9%` in EventProf; `42.86s` in `TriggerWebhookWorker` alone across `3,829` calls)
- **Fabrication (`FactoryProf`)**: `4,721` total calls (`3,243` top-level), `126.46s` (`89%` of total time)
  - `status`: `1,003` calls (`68.30s`, `68.1ms`/call)

  - `notification`: `76` calls (`6.42s`, `84.5ms`/call)
  - `user`: `93` calls (`3.51s`, `37.7ms`/call)

### Root Causes Identified
1. **`TriggerWebhookWorker` running inline on every model save (`~30%` of runtime)**:
   - `spec/rails_helper.rb` enabled `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` globally.
   - `Account`, `User`, `Status`, and `Report` `after_commit` callbacks enqueue `TriggerWebhookWorker`.

2. **Verbose Rails debug/SQL logging in test (`~7.6%` of runtime + 123 MB `log/test.log`)**:
   - `config/environments/test.rb` had no `config.log_level`, defaulting to `:debug`.
   - `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql` formatted, colorized, and wrote every SQL query to `log/test.log`.

Use `refind: true` (not `reload: true`) for `let_it_be(:account, ...)` whenever the account may be mutated or queried for relationships.

1. **`config/environments/test.rb`**:

  # TODO: Remove when Devise fixes https://github.com/heartcombo/devise/issues/5705
  config.before :suite do
    Rails.application.reload_routes_unless_loaded
  end

  config.around(:each, use_transactional_tests: false) do |example|
    self.use_transactional_tests = false
    example.run
    self.use_transactional_tests = true
  end

  config.before do
    Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)
  end

  config.before :each, type: :model do |example|
    if example.metadata[:sidekiq_inline]
      Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)
    else
      Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)
      Sidekiq::Worker.clear_all
    end
  end

  config.before :each, type: :cli do
    stub_reset_connection_pools
  end

  config.before :each, type: :request do
    # Use https and configured hostname in request spec requests
    integration_session.https!
    host! Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
  end

  config.before :each, type: :system do
    # Align with capybara config so that rails helpers called from rspec use matching host
    host! 'localhost:3000'
  end

  config.after do
    Rails.cache.clear
    redis.del(redis.keys)
  end

  # Assign types based on dir name for non-inferred types
  config.define_derived_metadata(file_path: %r{/spec/}) do |metadata|
    unless metadata.key?(:type)

      metadata[:type] = match[1].singularize.to_sym

end

module TestProf
  # EventProf profiles your tests and suites against custom events,
  # such as ActiveSupport::Notifications.
  #
  # It works very similar to `rspec --profile` but can track arbitrary events.
  #
  # Example:
  #
  #   # Collect SQL queries stats for every suite and example
  #   EVENT_PROF='sql.active_record' rspec ...
  #
  # By default it collects information only about top-level groups (aka suites),
  # but you can also profile individual examples. Just set the configuration option:
  #
  #  TestProf::EventProf.configure do |config|
  #    config.per_example = true
  #  end
  #
  # Or provide the EVENT_PROF_EXAMPLES=1 env variable.
  module EventProf
    # EventProf configuration
    class Configuration
      # Map of supported instrumenters
      INSTRUMENTERS = {
        active_support: "ActiveSupport"
      }.freeze

      attr_accessor :instrumenter, :top_count, :per_example,
        :rank_by, :event

      def initialize
        @event = ENV["EVENT_PROF"]
        @instrumenter = :active_support
        @top_count = (ENV["EVENT_PROF_TOP"] || 5).to_i
        @per_example = ENV["EVENT_PROF_EXAMPLES"] == "1"
        @rank_by = (ENV["EVENT_PROF_RANK"] || :time).to_sym
        @stamp = ENV["EVENT_PROF_STAMP"]

        RSpecStamp.config.tags = @stamp if stamp?
      end

      def stamp?
        !@stamp.nil?
      end

      def per_example?
        per_example == true
      end

      def resolve_instrumenter
        return instrumenter if instrumenter.is_a?(Module)

"
}

**Optimizing Request Spec Performance**

Okay, so I've been digging into the `spec/requests` directory, and I've zeroed in on `cache_spec.rb`. Looking at lines 174-184, I'm seeing a massive performance bottleneck. The `before` block there is a serious offender. It's creating a whole bunch of records (eleven, to be exact, plus a `follow!` and seven inline Sidekiq jobs!) for *every single* example – a whopping 258 times! The kicker is, none of those examples actually *mutate* those records. They're basically static, read-only fixtures for testing HTTP cache headers. This is a clear case for optimization.

My initial thought is that converting that `before` block to a `before_all` (using `let_it_be` or a regular `before_all`) is going to make a huge difference. Based on the current runtime of 49.21 seconds, I'm betting we can slash that down to around 5 seconds. I'll need to double-check the rest of `cache_spec.rb` to make sure nothing in lines 361+ is modifying these records, but I'm pretty confident in that initial assessment.

Now, to get a complete picture, I need to profile the *entire* `spec/requests` directory, excluding `cache_spec.rb` to isolate the impact of this change. I'm going to run the profiler with `FPROF=1 RD_PROF=1 RD_PROF_TOP=25 EVENT_PROF=sidekiq.inline EVENT_PROF_TOP=25` on everything under `spec/requests` except `cache_spec.rb`. I'm going to use the `bundle exec rspec -r test-prof $(find spec/requests -name "*_spec.rb" ! -name "cache_spec.rb" | sort)` command to exclude the one file. That should give me a solid baseline.

**Analyzing Performance Bottlenecks**

Okay, *whoa*, those profiling numbers are significant, even with the partial output! I need to dig deeper. My initial instinct is to run `FPROF=1` to get a full picture. Alternatively, I could capture the complete output of `RD_PROF=1` along with `FPROF=1` for non-`cache_spec.rb` requests and store it in `tmp/prof_requests.txt`. But, hold on, let's see what we already have.

Alright, here's a quick breakdown:
1.  **`EventProf` for `sidekiq.inline`**:

    *   Even the `cache_spec.rb` tests contribute significantly: **`00:27.766` (`31.31%`)**, with **1,806** events!

Now, let's broaden the scope. I want to see the top `RSpecDissect` and `Factories usage` data from this run, and, crucially, understand the `EVENT_PROF=sql.active_record` performance impact.

I'll run `FPROF=1 RD_PROF=1 RD_PROF_TOP=25` on the non-`cache_spec.rb` specs and write that to `tmp/prof_requests.txt`. This should provide me with the comprehensive data I need for a thorough analysis, and it should prevent any truncation of the results.

**Debugging and Tracing Sidekiq Interactions in the Codebase**

Alright, so I'm seeing a pattern here. I need to figure out the interactions between these services and the background jobs, especially when things fail in test environments, or when asynchronous behavior is interfering with synchronous tests. Let's see...

First, in `conversations_spec.rb`, it's straightforward: `PostStatusService.new.call(...)` kicks off `DistributionWorker`, which, aha!, creates `AccountConversation`. Clear connection there.

Then, things get more interesting in `favourites_spec.rb`. We have `FavouriteService.new.call(...)` followed by `status.account.block!(user.account)`. Wait a minute, why did the `unfavourite` test flake when using a fake Sidekiq? Could be one of a few things: maybe `status.account.block!(user.account)` is the culprit. Perhaps `BlockWorker` runs asynchronously and removes favourites. Or, maybe it's `NotificationWorker` causing the test to fail. Looks like tagging those specs with `:sidekiq_inline` should resolve the test failure.

Finally, in `home_spec.rb` we have a similar situation. Both `PostStatusService.new.call(...)` and `ReblogService.new.call(...)` enqueue `DistributionWorker`, which populates the Redis home feed. Got it.

And just to be thorough, I'm going to take a look at those three notifications specs as well to see if there are any related issues with asynchronous operations. Let's get a complete picture of these dependencies.

    Class.new(ApplicationController) do
      include SignatureVerification

      before_action :require_actor_signature!, only: [:signature_required]

      def success
        render json: {
          signed_request: signed_request?,
          signature_actor_id: signed_request_actor&.id&.to_s,
        }.merge(signature_verification_failure_reason || {})
      end

      alias_method :alternative_success, :success
      alias_method :signature_required, :success
    end
  end

  def digest_value(body)
    "SHA-256=#{Digest::SHA256.base64digest(body)}"
  end

  def build_signature_string(keypair, key_id, request_target, headers)
    algorithm = 'rsa-sha256'
    signed_headers = headers.merge({ '(request-target)' => request_target })
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")
    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(keypair.sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"#{algorithm}\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""
  end

  def build_signature_string(keypair, key_id, request_target, headers)
    algorithm = 'rsa-sha256'
    signed_headers = headers.merge({ '(request-target)' => request_target })
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")

I'm wondering if using `let_it_be(:user, refind: true)` in this shared context is safe. I need to ensure that it won't break any of the existing tests. I considered how this would interact with `before_all`, nested `before` blocks, and overridden `let` declarations. I also checked if any of the dependencies used in the `Fabricate` call have their own `let` definitions.

And then `signature_verification_spec.rb` also saw a huge boost, dropping from **8.13 seconds to a mere 0.83 seconds**, a **9.8x improvement** and shaving off 7.3 seconds! Now, let's address that lone failure in `signature_verification_spec.rb:149`. Ah, right, that `context 'when the key material has changed'` is the culprit. It's trying to get a different public key for `actor` within a nested context, but it's re-initializing a new `actor` with the same identifying attributes. That's inefficient and likely the source of the test failure, because it seems to be accidentally creating and persisting a second `bob` when we just want to update the existing one.

Instead of creating this redundant `let!(:actor)`, it's much cleaner to simply update the existing `actor`'s `public_key`. I can just use `actor.update!` with a new key. Thinking through the best way to generate that new key, I want to avoid unnecessary database writes, so I can use `Fabricate.build(:account)` to get a default public key. Or better yet, I can use `Fabricate.build(:account, domain: 'other.example').public_key` to avoid even accidentally re-using an existing account. Since we're inside a transaction, the changes will roll back cleanly at the end of the test.

I'm confident that this fix in `spec/requests/signature_verification_spec.rb` will resolve the failure and that both files will pass with flying colors. I'm going to implement that change and then verify that all tests in both files are passing without failures.

messages.thinking:
**Optimizing Reply and Notification Specs**

Okay, let's dive into these specs and see if we can streamline things. First, looking at `spec/requests/activitypub/replies_spec.rb`, the sheer number of statuses being fabricated is screaming for optimization. We're creating **7 statuses** for every single example, and we have 45 examples. That's a whopping **315 statuses**, plus extra in the cases with self-replies, and it's all in the `before` block. We need to reduce this duplication.

The structure reveals some opportunities. We have three main visibility scenarios: `:public`, `:private`, and `:direct`. Most examples use `:public`, and the replies are *identical* across those examples, except for mutations to the account within the example transaction. That’s key. We can factor this out.  We're also constantly fabricating `remote_account` and `remote_querier`. Why not define those just *once*?

My initial thought is that we could create *three* status trees in a `before_all` block (or, better yet, `let_it_be`) – one for each visibility – and then reuse them. The `let_it_be` calls seem perfect for this, as they will be reloaded and are scoped to the example group. We would then fetch the appropriate tree based on `parent_visibility` in the individual examples. I could create a helper method, `create_thread(visibility)`, to generate the initial status and its replies.

Wait, hold on... the `uri: remote_reply_id` assignment in the test. If Status has a unique index or validation on the `uri` column, then that would cause a problem with creating three status trees with the same `remote_reply_id`. We'll need to check the model to see if the `uri` is unique, if it's not, we'll need to modify the code to take this into account.

Okay, I see: the `uri` is only needed in the public case. We can generate a unique `uri` in the other cases, perhaps `"https://foobar.com/statuses/#{vis}"`.

If we can refactor this way, we can fabricate only *21* statuses (3 visibilities * 7 status/replies) instead of 315+. That should save a *ton* of time. We need to remember that `stub_const 'ActivityPub::RepliesController::DESCENDANTS_LIMIT', 5` still needs to be in the `before` block, but that's fine.

Now, let's also take a look at the notification specs: `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications_spec.rb`, and `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb` to see if we can apply the same optimization strategies there. I need to read through the `v1` and `v2` specs to understand their structure and identify any similar patterns of redundant setup.

**Optimizing Notification Spec Tests**

Okay, I've taken a look at `spec/requests/api/v1/notifications_spec.rb`, `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications_spec.rb`, and `spec/requests/api/v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb`. It's pretty clear where we can make significant speed improvements.

In all three spec files, both the `GET .../unread_count` and `GET .../notifications` endpoints have a `before` block that sets up a common scenario by creating `first_status` and five notifications using `PostStatusService`, `ReblogService`, `FavouriteService`, and `FollowService`. The problem is, these services are being re-run for *every* example within each `describe` block. I’ve noticed the tests are slow - the total is around **15.25 seconds**!

What's causing the slowdown is that all the notification creation services are executed, with `Sidekiq::Testing.inline!` called within each example. This means we're essentially re-creating the same notifications over and over.

Here's the plan to optimize:

First, let's convert `bob` and `tom` to use `let_it_be(..., refind: true)` to share the instances across the tests.

Second, we can wrap the entire setup `before_all` block within `Sidekiq::Testing.inline! { ... }`. This will ensure the services run only *once* for each `describe` block, drastically cutting down on redundant processing. We also need to remove any top-level `:sidekiq_inline` tags from the `RSpec.describe` block.

But, before we make global changes, we need to check if any specific examples *require* `:sidekiq_inline`.

In `v2/notifications_spec.rb` on line 314, there is a `before` block that explicitly calls `FavouriteService`, so we will need to keep `:sidekiq_inline` for that example.

Then, I'll review lines 90-230 of `v2/notifications_spec.rb` (which were elided) and lines 210-240 of `v1/notifications_spec.rb` to make sure we didn't miss any notifications being created.

For `v1/notifications_spec.rb`, the `user` is currently defined with `let(:user)`, and is overridden, but it's *already* using `let_it_be(:user, refind: true)`! The fix here is to change the overridden definition to `let_it_be(:user, refind: true)`. This will share the `user` across all examples, and we can move the notification creation to a `before_all` block (wrapped in `Sidekiq::Testing.inline!`).

We’ll do the same in `v2/notifications_spec.rb`: change `let(:user)`, `let(:bob)`, and `let(:tom)` to `let_it_be(:user, refind: true)`, `let_it_be(:bob, refind: true)`, and `let_it_be(:tom, refind: true)` respectively, and wrap the notification setup in `before_all` with `Sidekiq::Testing.inline!`.

Finally, for `v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb`, we'll convert `let(:token)` to `let_it_be(:token, refind: true)` and do the same `before_all` and `Sidekiq::Testing.inline!` wrapping.

To ensure we don't miss anything, let me review the sections in the files I mentioned.

**Optimizing Notifications Specs: A Deep Dive**

Okay, let's get down to brass tacks. I'm looking at these spec files and seeing some low-hanging fruit for performance improvement. The core idea here is to leverage `before_all` blocks and inline Sidekiq where appropriate, to reduce test execution time.

First, in `api/v1/notifications_spec.rb`, the patterns are clear. Replace the `before` blocks with `before_all` where applicable for the unread count and notifications endpoints and get rid of the `:sidekiq_inline` tag. I'm double-checking the end of this file (lines 250+) just to make sure I don't miss any dependencies or edge cases.

Next, `api/v2/notifications_spec.rb` is showing similar patterns. I'm swapping `before` for `before_all` in the unread count and main notification descriptions and cleaning up the `:sidekiq_inline` tags. The nested `before_all` block in the 'numerous notifications' context is a little trickier. My initial instinct was to replace it, but that's a common area for test pollution. If `use_transactional_tests = true`, `before_all` opens a transaction at the start of the `context` and rolls it back at the end of the `context`! So, `user.account.notifications.destroy_all` inside that nested `before_all` WILL be rolled back when the inner context finishes. I'll verify this by running the spec with both `--order defined` and `--order random` to be sure. And for `api/v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb`, replace the `before` with `before_all` and remove the `:sidekiq_inline`.

Now, things get a bit more interesting with the timelines. `home_spec.rb` and `conversations_spec.rb` require closer attention. I can see the `let_it_be` definitions there, and the `before_all` block. Ah, the Redis dependency! The `config.after` block in `rails_helper.rb` clears Redis *after each example*. If I use `before_all` in `home_spec.rb`, the Redis data will be wiped after the *first* example, which will cause the remaining examples to fail as the Home Feed is wiped. So I must keep the `before` block (with `:sidekiq_inline`) because of the Redis dependency. But wait, `conversations_spec.rb` uses Postgres (`AccountConversation`)! I should be able to cleanly swap the `before` for `before_all` in that one.

**Refactoring Test Suites with `let_it_be` and `before_all`**

Okay, so I'm looking at these four spec files – `public_spec.rb`, `link_spec.rb`, `tag_spec.rb`, and `outboxes_spec.rb` – and they're looking pretty clean. Time to get them updated and standardized! I'm thinking, let's convert those over to using `let_it_be` and `before_all`. That should give us a nice performance boost and make the test setup more explicit.

Hang on a sec... I'm noticing something interesting in `outboxes_spec.rb`. Look at these lines: `account.suspend!`, `account.mark_deleted!`, `account.block!`, and `remote_account.follow!(account)`. The key here is the `refind: true` option on both `account` and `remote_account`. Because of this, each example effectively gets a fresh, reloaded record after the transactional rollback. This is a great pattern!

And then, over in `link_spec.rb`, I see the "when there is no preview card" section with `let(:preview_card) { nil }`. Now, if we swap that to use `let_it_be(:preview_card, refind: true) { Fabricate(:preview_card, url: url) }` *and* use `before_all` to create a `trend` and `PreviewCardsStatus`, then we can replace that specific test block with a `before { preview_card.destroy! }` inside that example's transaction, and be confident that the `PreviewCard.find_by(url: url)` will be nil when checked (and will rollback cleanly afterwards!). Clean, elegant, and efficient.

Okay, that's the plan. I'm going to apply those edits – the `let_it_be`/`before_all` approach and the `refind: true` goodness for cleanup – to `public_spec.rb`, `link_spec.rb`, `tag_spec.rb`, and `outboxes_spec.rb`, and then run them. I'm feeling confident about this. Let's see how they perform!

Aha! Got it! That bug in `link_spec.rb:145`... what a fantastic find! I see the issue now. In the original code, the `before` block in `link_spec.rb` evaluated `remote_status` before `local_status`. That established an initial order of creation: `remote_status.id < local_status.id`.

However, the `let_it_be` declarations were defined in the *opposite* order! `local_status` was declared before `remote_status` (line 32 vs 33). This meant when the examples ran, the `let_it_be` calls were establishing a *different* order: `local_status.id < remote_status.id`.

The fix is straightforward, and the performance gain is immediately apparent: swapping the evaluation order within the `before` block or, equivalently, reordering the `let_it_be` declarations. Ensuring the creation order is consistent – `remote_status` created first, then `local_status` – solves the problem.

And the best part? Look at the numbers! Total run time for those four files has plummeted from 12.70 seconds to a mere 1.97 seconds – a whopping 6.4x speedup! Amazing.

Time to apply this fix to `link_spec.rb` and verify that all 48 examples still pass. This is going to be a good one!

ruby -e '
  path = "spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/link_spec.rb"
  text = File.read(path)
  old = [
    "    let_it_be(:local_status, refind: true) { Fabricate(:status, account: Fabricate.build(:account, domain: nil, discoverable: true)) }",
    "    let_it_be(:remote_status, refind: true) { Fabricate(:status, account: Fabricate.build(:account, domain: '\''example.com'\'', discoverable: true)) }",
  ].join("\n")
  new = [
    "    let_it_be(:remote_status, refind: true) { Fabricate(:status, account: Fabricate.build(:account, domain: '\''example.com'\'', discoverable: true)) }",
    "    let_it_be(:local_status, refind: true) { Fabricate(:status, account: Fabricate.build(:account, domain: nil, discoverable: true)) }",
  ].join("\n")
  raise "not found" unless text.include?(old)
  File.write(path, text.sub(old, new))
' && bundle exec rspec \

  spec/requests/api/v1/timelines/link_spec.rb \

**Incredible Speedup!**

Wow, check out that result! The tests finished in a lightning-fast **57.12 seconds**!  And even better, the file loading was only a small fraction of the time, just **1.81 seconds**.  We had **1877 examples** with **0 failures**! This is a massive improvement.

Remember how it used to take **3 minutes and 15.7 seconds (195.7s)**? We've knocked that down to **57.12s** - that's a whopping **70.8% faster**, or a **3.43x speedup**!

Let's break it down further. Combining the `spec/models` and `spec/requests` times, the baseline used to be **340.8s** (5m 40.8s), with 145.1s from models and 195.7s from requests. Now, it's down to a mere **97.21s** (1m 37.2s), with 40.09s for models and 57.12s for requests. That's a **3.5x faster** combined suite!

This is excellent!  But, now that `spec/requests` runs so quickly, in under a minute, I think we can squeeze even more performance out. We can run profiling. messages.thinking:
**Analyzing Factory Usage in `spec/requests`**

Okay, let's break this down. First, I'm looking at the before-and-after factory usage in the `spec/requests` directory. The baseline shows a staggering **11,030** total factories being used, with **6,561** being top-level, and a runtime of 211.04s. Now, post-optimization, the total has plummeted to **5,304** (with 3,524 top-level) at 32.95s! That's a huge reduction, a significant improvement. I'm seeing dramatic drops across several key factories: `status` has dropped 66.6%, `user` down 43.3%, `moderator_user` down an incredible 99.6%, and so on. This reduction is substantial.

I'm also going to check the top 10 suites in `RSpecDissect` from that run, which is something I want to do on every run. I need exact post-optimization metrics to keep `docs/test_suite_optimization.md` accurate, and I want to see if there's any other big, common pattern that we've missed.

I'm now going to run some more checks; specifically, I need to look at the top 15 suites in `RD_PROF=1`. I'll also be searching the `spec/requests/` directory for any other shared authentication patterns. I'm especially interested in files that define `let(:user)`, `let(:token)`, and `let(:headers)` without also including a specific `'with API authentication'` description. That could be a hint as to an area where we can further optimize.

arguments.command: RD_PROF=1 RD_PROF_TOP=15 EVENT_PROF=sql.active_record EVENT_PROF_TOP=10 bundle exec rspec -r test-prof spec/requests --format progress | tail -n 100

messages.content: Let's update `accounts_spec.rb`, `statuses_spec.rb`, `api/v1/admin/accounts_spec.rb`, `api/v1/admin/reports_spec.rb`, `api/v2/admin/accounts_spec.rb`, and `api/v1/profiles_spec.rb` to use `let_it_be`/`before_all`, and run them.
messages.thinking:
**Optimizing Test Performance with `let_it_be(:..., refind: true)`**

Okay, let's see if we can significantly speed up these tests. I've been looking at the test suite, and I've identified several areas ripe for optimization using `let_it_be` with the `refind: true` option.

Specifically, I'm thinking about `accounts_spec.rb`, particularly the `with RSS` section. That section alone generates a lot of data, creating eight statuses, media attachments, and pinned statuses across four examples. With how `let_it_be` and `before_all` are used in `with RSS` and at the top of the file, this should really benefit from the change.

I'm also seeing similar opportunities in `statuses_spec.rb` where we can use `let_it_be(:account, refind: true)` and `let_it_be(:status, refind: true)`. And in `admin/reports_spec.rb`, we can apply `let_it_be` with `refind: true` to the reporter and spammer and the `before_all` block.

Even in the admin sections, I'm noticing that `admin/accounts_spec.rb` and `v2/admin/accounts_spec.rb` have opportunities to optimize by applying `let_it_be` to accounts!

And let's not forget `profiles_spec.rb`, which also uses `let_it_be(:account)`. This should make all of those files run way faster.

I'm ready to make those changes and test the six files I've mentioned!

messages.thinking:
**Analyzing These Test Failures**

Okay, these three failures are giving me some real insights into our testing setup. Let's break them down.

Firstly, regarding `api/v1/profiles_spec.rb`, the random order of test execution, specifically with Paperclip file attachments, is exposing a crucial flaw. Deleting a profile header (which also deletes the file on disk) before the avatar (and its deletion) in the spec file leads to the test failing. The database transactions are rolling back database changes, but *not* file system changes. I need to be careful with `let_it_be` when dealing with Paperclip attachments. I need to revert the use of `let_it_be` for the `account` in `profiles_spec.rb` because of the file deletions.

Next, looking at `api/v2/admin/accounts_spec.rb`, the order of evaluation with `let_it_be` is biting me. Because of where `let_it_be(:user)` was defined, the `admin_account` ended up with the *smallest* ID instead of the expected largest. This is a subtle but important detail. The suggested solution: move `let_it_be(:user)` to the correct location or keep `let(:user)` as-is in the test. The current test suite structure with `v2/admin/accounts_spec.rb` has just a few tests. Keeping the existing `let(:user)` is the simplest solution! Also, the primary issue is the order of `let_it_be` calls, not efficiency.

Finally, `statuses_spec.rb` is giving me some head-scratchers. Five failures in the "when signed in" context... why? After some quick investigation, the problem seems to be linked to how we're handling `user` and `account`. I remembered the "gotcha" about `Account` caching and relationship state. That's why we're using `refind: true`. However, that wasn't enough to fix it! I noticed in `statuses_spec.rb` that the `sign_in_with_session(user)` call on line 150. There's a possible side effect in `sign_in_with_session(user)` or the way that `let(:status)` overrides `let_it_be(:status)` which is causing the incorrect status codes to be returned.

messages.thinking:
**Eureka! A Debugging Breakthrough!**

Okay, here's the deal. I was digging into `sign_in_with_session(user)` and it hit me: the way we're handling the `user` object with `let_it_be(:user, refind: true)` is creating a problem. When we call `User.find(user.id)`, we're losing the `user.password` attribute. That's because the password is just an `attr_accessor` set during object creation with `Fabricate(:user)`. It's not persisted to the database. So, `post user_session_path` was failing to sign in! No wonder those tests were intermittently failing; the `refind: true` call was causing the missing password!

This is a fantastic catch, actually! It's a subtle but critical distinction in how our test setup interacts with the database.

Now, let's get this fixed. In `statuses_spec.rb`, the `when signed in` block needs a reliable `user.password` – whether we explicitly pass it, or keep the original `let(:user)` setup to ensure the password exists. Or, as an alternative (and potentially cleaner solution!), while keeping `let(:user) { Fabricate(:user) }` in `when signed in`, we can apply `let_it_be` to `account`, `status` and `remote_account`.

I'm thinking we can revert the changes in `profiles_spec.rb` and, in `v2/admin/accounts_spec.rb`, we'll keep `let(:user)`, and in `statuses_spec.rb`, we'll keep `let(:user)` but change `remote_account` to `let_it_be`. Then, we'll re-run all those six files and verify that this completely resolves the sign-in issue. I have a feeling this will solve those pesky, intermittent test failures.

# Test Suite Optimization Notes & Plan

## Phase 1: `spec/models` + Global Configuration

### Baseline Metrics (`spec/models` — 1,795 examples)
- **Clean runtime**: `2m 25.1s` (145.1s)
- **RSpecDissect**: `141.5s` total, `116.3s` (82.2%) in setup
- **SQL (`sql.active_record`)**: `113,956` queries (`22.43s`, ~63.5 queries/example)
- **Sidekiq inline jobs (`sidekiq.inline`)**: `3,908` inline job executions (`37.70s` / `26.9%` in EventProf; `42.86s` in `TriggerWebhookWorker` alone across `3,829` calls)
- **Fabrication (`FactoryProf`)**: `4,721` total calls (`3,243` top-level), `126.46s` (`89%` of total time)
  - `status`: `1,003` calls (`68.30s`, `68.1ms`/call)
  - `bookmark`: `1,019` calls (`17` top-level, `34.67s`, `34.0ms`/call — triggered by `Fabricate(:status)` `after_create`)
  - `account`: `1,194` calls (`31.51s`, `26.4ms`/call)
  - `media_attachment`: `40` calls (`6.27s`, `156.7ms`/call)
  - `notification`: `76` calls (`6.42s`, `84.5ms`/call)
  - `user`: `93` calls (`3.51s`, `37.7ms`/call)

### Root Causes Identified
1. **`TriggerWebhookWorker` running inline on every model save (`~30%` of runtime)**:
   - `spec/rails_helper.rb` enabled `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` globally.
   - `Account`, `User`, `Status`, and `Report` `after_commit` callbacks enqueue `TriggerWebhookWorker`.
   - Even with 0 `Webhook` rows in the DB, `TriggerWebhookWorker` reloaded the record from Postgres and serialized the full payload via `REST::Admin::WebhookEventSerializer` before discovering `Webhook.enabled...pluck(:id)` was empty.
   - Out of 1,795 model examples, only 3 failed under `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` — all 3 used `ActionMailer::TestHelper#capture_emails`, which relies on `deliver_later` executing immediately.
2. **Verbose Rails debug/SQL logging in test (`~7.6%` of runtime + 123 MB `log/test.log`)**:
   - `config/environments/test.rb` had no `config.log_level`, defaulting to `:debug`.
   - `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql` formatted, colorized, and wrote every SQL query to `log/test.log`.
3. **Stray `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` in a spec file**:
   - `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb:6` left `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` enabled globally, polluting all subsequent examples with stacktrace collection per SQL query.
4. **Per-example `rails_helper.rb` overhead**:
   - `Rails.application.reload_routes_unless_loaded` ran before every single example (~1.88ms/call, ~3.4s in `spec/models`, ~18s+ across the full suite).
   - `allow(Resolv::DNS).to receive(:open)...` ran `rspec-mocks` setup/teardown before every example.
5. **Repeated DB setup in slow model specs**:
   - Suites like `AccountStatusesCleanupPolicy`, `TagFeed`, `PublicFeed`, `Trends::Statuses`, `Status`, `Notification`, `Status::ThreadingConcern`, `Status::FetchRepliesConcern`, `Account::Interactions`, `Form::Import`, etc. recreated large graphs of `Status`/`Account`/`Tag` records per example via `let`/`let!`/`before`.
   - **Important codebase gotcha for `let_it_be` with `Account`**: `Account` caches `account_stat` association state (`Account::Counters#update_count!` checks `association(:account_stat).loaded?`) AND memoizes relationship ivars (`@following`, `@blocking`, `@muting`, `@domain_blocking`). Use `refind: true` (not `reload: true`) for `let_it_be(:account, ...)` whenever the account may be mutated or queried for relationships.

### Changes Applied in Phase 1
1. **`config/environments/test.rb`**:
   - Set `config.log_level = ENV.fetch('RAILS_LOG_LEVEL', :warn)`.
2. **`spec/rails_helper.rb`**:
   - Required `test_prof/recipes/rspec/let_it_be` (enables `let_it_be` and `before_all`).
   - Moved `Rails.application.reload_routes_unless_loaded` from `config.before` to `config.before :suite`.
   - Replaced per-example `allow(Resolv::DNS).to receive(:open)` mock with a lightweight singleton guard on `Resolv::DNS.open` (respects `type: :system` and `rspec-mocks` stubbing).
   - Added `SidekiqInlineCaptureEmails` wrapping `ActionMailer::TestHelper#capture_emails` in `Sidekiq::Testing.inline!`.
   - Set `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` + `Sidekiq::Worker.clear_all` in `config.before :each, type: :model` (with `:sidekiq_inline` tag opt-in).
3. **`spec/models/**/*_spec.rb` & `spec/support/examples/models/concerns/reviewable.rb`**:
   - Removed stray `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` from `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`.
   - Converted repeated shared setup in the slowest model specs (`account_statuses_cleanup_policy_spec.rb`, `tag_feed_spec.rb`, `public_feed_spec.rb`, `trends/statuses_spec.rb`, `status_spec.rb`, `notification_spec.rb`, `concerns/status/threading_concern_spec.rb`, `concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`, `concerns/account/interactions_spec.rb`, `form/import_spec.rb`, `account_spec.rb`, `account_suggestions/friends_of_friends_source_spec.rb`, `admin/account_action_spec.rb`, `collection_spec.rb`, `concerns/account/mappings_spec.rb`, `form/custom_emoji_batch_spec.rb`, `status/visibility_spec.rb`, `status_pin_spec.rb`, `web/push_subscription_spec.rb`, `account/search_spec.rb`, and `reviewable.rb`) to `let_it_be` / `before_all`.

### Phase 1 Results (`spec/models` — 1,795 examples, 0 failures)
- **Clean runtime**: `145.1s` -> **`40.09s`** (and `33.4s` post-Phase 2; **>72% faster / 3.6x+ speedup**)
- **SQL queries**: `113,956` -> `44,916` (**-60.6%**)
- **Factory calls**: `4,721` (`126.46s`) -> `2,809` (`34.66s`) (**-40.5% calls, -72.6% time**)
- **Per-call `status` time**: `68.1ms` -> `27.5ms` (**-60%**)
- **Per-call `account` time**: `26.4ms` -> `13.2ms` (**-50%**)

## Phase 2: `spec/requests`

### Baseline Metrics (`spec/requests` — 1,877 examples)
- **Clean runtime**: `3m 15.7s` (`195.7s`)
- **ActionController execution (`process_action.action_controller`)**: Only ~6–11% of runtime in slow suites (`cache_spec.rb`: `11.1%`, `replies_spec.rb`: `5.9%`); ~80–99% of runtime was test setup & inline Sidekiq execution.
- **Sidekiq inline jobs (`sidekiq.inline`)**: `7,592` inline job executions across `spec/requests` (`1,806` in `cache_spec.rb` = `27.77s` / `31.3%`; `5,786` in the rest = `68.21s` / `32.6%`).
- **Fabrication (`FactoryProf`)**: `11,030` total calls (`6,561` top-level) across `spec/requests`:
  - `cache_spec.rb` alone: `2,849` calls (`1,817` top-level, `75.37s` in prof / `49.21s` clean)
  - Remaining 262 files: `8,181` calls (`4,744` top-level, `135.67s` in prof)
  - Top factories: `status` (1,450), `bookmark` (1,459), `user` (939), `admin_user` (281), `moderator_user` (258), `account` (1,070), `accessible_access_token` (1,166), `login_activity` (2,970).
- **Top baseline suites**: `cache_spec.rb` (`49.21s` / 258 ex), `activitypub/replies_spec.rb` (`16.82s` / 45 ex), `signature_verification_spec.rb` (`8.13s` / 30 ex), `api/v2/notifications_spec.rb` (`7.62s` / 29 ex), `api/v1/notifications_spec.rb` (`5.86s` / 22 ex), `api/v1/timelines/public_spec.rb` (`4.07s` / 12 ex), `activitypub/contexts_spec.rb` (`3.92s` / 7 ex), `api/v1/timelines/link_spec.rb` (`3.51s` / 11 ex), `activitypub/outboxes_spec.rb` (`3.08s` / 14 ex).

### Root Causes Identified
1. **`Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` still active for `type: :request` (~32% of runtime)**:
   - Out of 1,877 request examples, only 35 examples across 6 files failed under `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)`:
     - `api/v1/conversations_spec.rb` (`PostStatusService` -> `DistributionWorker` creates `AccountConversation`)
     - `api/v1/statuses/favourites_spec.rb` (`UnfavouriteWorker`)
     - `api/v1/timelines/home_spec.rb` (`PostStatusService`/`ReblogService` -> `DistributionWorker` populates Redis `HomeFeed`)
     - `api/v1/notifications_spec.rb`, `api/v2/notifications_spec.rb`, `api/v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb` (`PostStatusService`/`ReblogService`/`FavouriteService`/`FollowService` -> notification workers)
2. **Repeated `with API authentication` user fabrication (70 request spec files, 759 examples)**:
   - `spec/support/api_authentication.rb` fabricated a fresh `User` (`+ Account + 2 LoginActivity + BCrypt`) on every example.
3. **Massive per-example fixture graph in `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb` (258 examples, 25% of baseline)**:
   - `before` fabricated 11 records (`account`, `moderator_user`, 2 `status`es, `invite`, `poll`, `accessible_access_token`, `follow!`, plus nested `bookmark`/`login_activity`) for all 258 read-only `GET` examples, plus repeated `remote_actor` setups in 4 signature contexts.
4. **Full Mastodon routes reloaded 30 times in `spec/requests/signature_verification_spec.rb`**:
   - `before { stub_tests_controller }` + `after { Rails.application.reload_routes! }` re-drew and re-compiled the entire application route set after every single example.
5. **Repeated DB setup in slow request specs (`replies_spec.rb`, `notifications_spec.rb`, `contexts_spec.rb`, `timelines/*_spec.rb`, `outboxes_spec.rb`, `collections_spec.rb`, `accounts_spec.rb`, `statuses_spec.rb`, `admin/*_spec.rb`, etc.)**.
   - **Codebase gotchas for `let_it_be` in request specs**:
     - **Redis-backed feeds (`home_spec.rb`)**: `config.after` in `rails_helper.rb` runs `redis.del(redis.keys)` after every example, so Redis-backed setup (`HomeFeed`) must stay per-example (`before` + `:sidekiq_inline`), not `before_all`.
     - **Paperclip disk deletions (`api/v1/profiles_spec.rb`)**: DB transactions do not restore files deleted from `spec/test_files/` by `DELETE /api/v1/profile/avatar` or `/header`, so accounts with Paperclip attachments under deletion tests cannot use `let_it_be`.
     - **In-memory `user.password` (`statuses_spec.rb`)**: `sign_in_with_session` reads `user.password`, which is nil after `refind: true` (`User.find`). Keep `let(:user)` per-example when tests post `user.password` to `user_session_path`.
     - **Creation ID ordering (`link_spec.rb`, `v2/admin/accounts_spec.rb`)**: `let_it_be` evaluates in declaration order; preserve creation order when tests assert cursor pagination `min_id`/`max_id` against specific record IDs.

### Changes Applied in Phase 2
1. **`spec/rails_helper.rb`**:
   - Extended `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` + `Sidekiq::Worker.clear_all` (with `:sidekiq_inline` opt-in) to `type: :request` alongside `type: :model`.
2. **`spec/support/api_authentication.rb`**:
   - Changed `let(:user)` to `let_it_be(:user, refind: true)` across all 70 request spec files including `'with API authentication'`.
3. **`spec/requests/cache_spec.rb`**:
   - Converted shared top-level fixture graph and `remote_actor` contexts to `let_it_be(..., refind: true)` and `before_all` (`49.21s` -> `~3.7s`).
4. **`spec/requests/signature_verification_spec.rb`**:
   - Moved `stub_tests_controller` and `Rails.application.reload_routes!` from per-example `before`/`after` to `before(:all)`/`after(:all)`, and converted `actor_keypair` and `actor` to `let_it_be` (`8.13s` -> `~0.8s`).
5. **Notification & Conversation specs**:
   - `api/v1/notifications_spec.rb`, `api/v2/notifications_spec.rb`, `api/v2/notifications/accounts_spec.rb`, `api/v1/conversations_spec.rb`: converted shared user/notification setup to `let_it_be(..., refind: true)` + `before_all { Sidekiq::Testing.inline! { ... } }`, reserving `:sidekiq_inline` only for contexts that mutate/enqueue during individual examples.
   - Tagged `:sidekiq_inline` on `api/v1/statuses/favourites_spec.rb` (`POST /unfavourite`) and `api/v1/timelines/home_spec.rb` (`when the timeline is available`).
6. **Other slowest request specs converted to `let_it_be` / `before_all`**:
   - `activitypub/replies_spec.rb` (pre-built the 3 visibility status trees once via `let_it_be`), `activitypub/contexts_spec.rb`, `activitypub/outboxes_spec.rb`, `activitypub/collections_spec.rb`, `api/v1/timelines/public_spec.rb`, `api/v1/timelines/link_spec.rb`, `api/v1/timelines/tag_spec.rb`, `accounts_spec.rb`, `statuses_spec.rb`, `api/v1/admin/accounts_spec.rb`, `api/v1/admin/reports_spec.rb`, `api/v2/admin/accounts_spec.rb`, `api/v2/filters/statuses_spec.rb`, `api/v1/statuses/quotes_spec.rb`.

### Phase 2 Results (`spec/requests` — 1,877 examples, 0 failures)
- **Clean runtime**: `195.7s` (`3m 15.7s`) -> **`56.69s`** (**71.0% faster / 3.45x speedup**)
- **Sidekiq inline jobs**: `7,592` (`~96s` prof) -> `230` (`2.22s`, `3.9%`) (**-97.0% calls**)
- **Factory calls**: `11,030` (`6,561` top-level) -> `5,304` (`3,524` top-level, `32.95s` prof) (**-51.9% total calls**)
- **Combined `spec/models` + `spec/requests` runtime**: `340.8s` (`5m 40.8s`) -> **`90.09s`** (`1m 30.1s`, **73.6% faster / 3.78x speedup**)

## Plan for Future Phases

### Phase 3: Factories (`spec/fabricators/`)
Observations from Phase 1 & Phase 2 profiling (for when factories are in scope):
1. **`spec/fabricators/status_fabricator.rb`**:
   - `after_create { |status| Fabricate(:bookmark, status: status) }` creates an extra `bookmark` + a SECOND `account` + a SECOND `user` (with BCrypt hashing!) + TWO `login_activity` records on EVERY `Fabricate(:status)` call! That still accounted for `485` of `494` `bookmark` calls in Phase 2 (`5.5s`) and doubled `account`/`user`/`login_activity` creation.
2. **`spec/fabricators/user_fabricator.rb`**:
   - `after_create { |user| 2.times { Fabricate(:login_activity, user: user) } }` creates 2 `login_activity` rows on every `User` (and every local `Account`, since `account_fabricator` builds a `:user`!).
   - `password '123456789'` runs `BCrypt::Password.create` (`cost = 4`, ~3.2-4.3% of total CPU time) on every `User` / local `Account`. Precomputing a static `encrypted_password` hash for `'123456789'` (when password isn't overridden) would eliminate BCrypt overhead from `Fabricate(:account)` / `Fabricate(:user)` completely!
3. **`spec/fabricators/account_fabricator.rb`**:
   - `user { |attrs| attrs[:domain].nil? ? Fabricate.build(:user, account: nil) : nil }` forces a `User` (and 2 `login_activity` rows + BCrypt hash) to be created for every local `Account`, even when tests don't need a `User`.
4. **Default `TestProf::FactoryDefault` (`test_prof/recipes/rspec/factory_default`)**:
   - Can also reduce implicit parent creations in nested fabricators (`bookmark`, `notification`, `status`, etc.).
